hero.title: Mercedes-AMG M157 Engine - Replacement Cost, Problems & Compatibility
hero.description: The M157 is Mercedes-AMG’s legendary 5.5-litre V8 biturbo petrol engine, famous for its colossal torque, direct injection (CGI) technology, and the iconic "One Man, One Engine" hand-built philosophy. Fitted to the W221/W222 S-Class, W212 E-Class, and W166 GLE, reconditioned M157 engines typically start from £5,000 , serving as a highly sought-after unit for modern classic AMG restorations and performance builds.

costGuide.title: Mercedes-AMG M157 Engine Replacement Cost (UK)
costGuide.labourLine: Fitting an M157 engine typically takes 14-20 hours at £75-£95/hr (AMG specialist) - confirm exact labour when comparing quotes.
paragraphs: What genuinely moves the price for this engine is the condition of the twin turbochargers (specifically wastegate play), the high-pressure fuel pump (HPFP), and intake valve carbon buildup. Because the M157 is a complex, hand-built AMG unit, reputable recon specialists will typically test and refurbish the turbos, replace the HPFP, and perform a walnut blast carbon cleaning as standard to prevent immediate post-installation failures. For a full breakdown of market rates, see our full reconditioned engine cost guide.

failures.title: Mercedes-AMG M157 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: High-Pressure Fuel Pump (HPFP) Failure
items.whatHappens: The mechanical HPFP, driven by the camshaft, can suffer from internal wear or seal degradation. This leads to low fuel rail pressure, resulting in rough idling, long cranking times, misfires, and illuminated check engine lights.
items.repairVsReplace: Replacing the HPFP is a known, moderately labour-intensive repair. If ignored, it can cause lean running conditions that may damage the catalytic converters or pistons.

items.title: Turbocharger Wastegate Rattle and Failure
items.whatHappens: The wastegate actuator rods and linkage pins can wear, causing a distinct metallic rattling or chattering noise on deceleration or at idle. Over time, this wear leads to boost leaks, inconsistent boost pressure, and limp mode.
items.repairVsReplace: Early-stage rattles can sometimes be mitigated with aftermarket clip fixes, but a permanent solution requires replacing the wastegate actuators or rebuilding/replacing the turbochargers entirely.

items.title: Intake Valve Carbon Buildup
items.whatHappens: As a direct injection (CGI) engine, fuel is sprayed directly into the combustion chamber, meaning it does not wash over the back of the intake valves. Over time, oil vapours from the PCV system bake onto the valves, causing restrictive carbon buildup.
items.repairVsReplace: This manifests as rough idle, hesitation, and reduced power. The definitive repair is a professional "walnut blasting" service to clean the intake ports and valves, which is highly recommended as preventative maintenance.

items.title: PCV Valve and Oil Cooler Seal Leaks
items.whatHappens: The PCV valve diaphragm can rupture, causing a loud whistling noise, rough idle, and excessive oil consumption. Additionally, the turbocharger oil feed and return line seals harden over time, leading to external oil leaks.
items.repairVsReplace: PCV valve replacement is a straightforward and inexpensive repair. Turbo oil seal replacement requires more labour but is essential to prevent oil dripping onto hot exhaust components.

failures.goodYearsLine: The M157 is widely regarded as a monumental achievement in AMG engineering, offering V12-level torque with V8 reliability. Units maintained with strict, frequent oil changes (every 5,000-7,000 miles) and premium fuel routinely exceed 150,000 miles without major internal bottom-end issues .

variants.title: M157 Sub-Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: ═══════════════════════════════════════ INTRO: The M157 family shares the same fundamental 5.5L DOHC twin-turbo V8 block architecture, but power output, intake manifolds, and engine management vary significantly depending on the chassis. Identifying your exact sub-code is mandatory, as fitting the wrong revision can lead to severe mechanical and ECU incompatibility. - Fitted to: S-Class W221 / W222 (S 63 AMG), E-Class W212 (E 63 AMG) - Key technical difference: The flagship high-output variant, featuring specific AMG engine management calibration, unique intake plumbing, and (in later W222 models) the "Performance Package" tune of 585 hp. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; the heavy S-Class chassis places sustained thermal load on the turbochargers, accelerating wastegate wear if not properly maintained. - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with the C 63 AMG (.985) variant due to different engine mounts, wiring harnesses, and ECU mapping. - Fitted to: CLS-Class C218 (CLS 63 AMG), GLE-Class W166 (GLE 63 AMG) - Key technical difference: A variant optimized for the sleek CLS coupe and the heavier GLE SUV, featuring revised accessory brackets, heavy-duty engine mounts, and specific cooling system routing. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; SUV applications may experience accelerated turbo oil seal wear due to extreme operating angles and higher under-hood temperatures. - Interchange note: Requires matching sump, oil pickup, and accessory drives; passenger car variants are not directly interchangeable with SUV specs without significant modification.

relatives.description: the legendary 6.2L naturally aspirated V8 that the M157 replaced in the flagship AMG lineup, trading raw displacement for a twin-turbocharged design that delivered superior low-end torque and thermal efficiency.

the modern 4.0L V8 biturbo that eventually replaced the M157 across the AMG range, introducing a "hot-vee" turbo layout, direct injection refinements, and even stricter emissions compliance while maintaining colossal power figures.

the variant of the M157 family specifically calibrated for the CLS 63 AMG and GLE 63 AMG, sharing the exact same 5.5L hand-built block but featuring distinct intake plumbing, cooling setups, and chassis-specific ECU mapping.

variants.closing: The engine code is stamped on the right-hand side of the cylinder block, near the oil filter housing, almost always accompanied by the handwritten signature plaque of the AMG engine builder. It will also be listed on your V5C logbook under "Engine Capacity" or visible via a VIN decode. Not sure? Enter your registration above for instant confirmation.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement M157 Engine - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used M157 engine makes sense only if it comes with verifiable, stamped service history and documented proof of recent HPFP replacement, turbocharger health checks, and intake valve carbon cleaning. Given the high-performance nature and complexity of these vehicles, buying a used unit with unknown history is a significant financial risk.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper reconditioned M157 engine is the sweet spot for most buyers. A reputable rebuild will proactively address the common failure points by refurbishing or replacing the twin turbochargers, fitting a new HPFP, performing a thorough carbon clean, and renewing all brittle valve cover and turbo oil seals, giving the engine a fresh, reliable lease on life.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full M157 engine rebuild is highly justified for low-mileage or collector W222 S 63 AMG or W212 E 63 AMG restorations where originality, matching numbers (and the builder's signature plaque), and maximum longevity are required. An upgraded rebuild should include line-boring the block, new pistons/rings, and a balanced crankshaft.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Sourcing and fitting through our vetted network ensures your M157 engine is installed by specialists familiar with hand-built AMG biturbo systems, backed by a nationwide warranty.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: Because the M157 is typically found in W221, W222, W212, and W166 vehicles valued between £10,000 and £35,000+ (with low-mileage examples commanding significantly higher premiums), a full replacement is generally financially viable and protects the asset's value. However, if the lowest viable replacement cost exceeds approximately 60% of the vehicle's current market value, evaluate the investment carefully .

Fitted costs generally range from £6,500 to £10,000 depending on the specialist, while used units can be found from £2,000 but carry a high financial risk due to the potential for high-pressure fuel pump and turbocharger wear. → Compare M157 engine replacement quotes today

items.question: What is the most common failure on the M157 engine?
items.answer: The most documented issues are high-pressure fuel pump (HPFP) failure, turbocharger wastegate rattle, and intake valve carbon buildup. The HPFP can cause low fuel rail pressure and misfires, while wastegate wear leads to boost leaks and limp mode. Carbon buildup is a natural byproduct of direct injection and requires periodic walnut blasting. → Get quotes for a rebuilt M157 with these issues resolved
